etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English spit, a shortening of despit (whence despite), from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from Latin dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”). Compare also Dutch spijt and German Spiet.

definitions.definition: Ill will or hatred toward another, accompanied with the desire to unjustifiably irritate, annoy, or thwart; a want to disturb or put out another; mild malice

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: This is the deadly spite that angers.

quote.citation: 1943 November – 1944 February (date written; published 1945 August 17), George Orwell [pseudonym; Eric Arthur Blair], Animal Farm […], London: Secker & Warburg, published May 1962, →OCLC:
quote.text: Out of spite, the human beings pretended not to believe that it was Snowball who had destroyed the windmill: they said that it had fallen down because the walls were too thin.

quote.citation: 2014, Emivita, By Any Means Necessary: My Personal Struggles with Good and Evil:
quote.text: sex with older men was a way to both internalize my spite towards my mother and to find security in a father figure I lacked with my own father.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene v]:
quote.text: "The time is out of joint: O cursed spite."

definitions.definition: (transitive) To treat maliciously; to try to hurt or thwart.
(transitive, obsolete) To be angry at; to hate.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: The Danes, then  […]  pagans, principally spited places of religion.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To fill with spite; to offend; to vex.

quote.citation: a. 1700 (date written), William Temple, “Some Thoughts upon Reviewing the Essay of Antient and Modern Learning”, in Miscellanea. The Third Part. […], London:  […]  Jonathan Swift, […] Benjamin Tooke, […], published 1701, →OCLC, pages 240–241:
quote.text: But the laſt and fatal Blow, given to that antient Learning, was in the time of Darius, Father of Xerxes, who with the reſt of the Perſians, ſpighted at the Magi, upon the Uſurpation of the Crown by one of their Number, (that counterfeited a younger Son of Cyrus after the Death of Cambyſes,) when he came to be ſetled in that Throne, endeavour'd to aboliſh, not only their Learning and Credit, but their Language too, by changing the old Aſſyrian Characters, and introducing thoſe of Perſia, which grew to be the common Uſe of that whole Empire.
